title: What venture capital is
body: Venture capital funds invest other people's money (from pension funds, endowments and wealthy families) into young, fast-growing companies in exchange for shares. Most investments fail; the fund makes its return from the few that become huge.

title: Funding stages
body: Startups raise money in rounds: pre-seed and seed (friends, angels, small funds) to build and test the product; Series A to scale something that works; Series B, C and later to expand fast. Each round usually happens at a higher valuation if the company has grown.

title: Pre-money and post-money
body: Pre-money valuation is what the company is worth before new cash; post-money = pre-money + investment. An investor putting 1 million into a company at 4 million pre-money owns 1 / 5 = 20% afterwards, not 25%.

title: Dilution
body: Each funding round creates new shares, so founders own a smaller percentage. That is fine if the company's value grows faster: 60% of a 10 million company is worth more than 100% of a 1 million one. Founders track the cap table to see who owns what.

title: Why VCs chase home runs
body: Venture returns follow a power law: one great company can return more than the whole rest of the fund. So VCs back startups that could become enormous, not ones likely to be merely good. A solid small business can be a great life but a bad VC investment.

title: Unicorns
body: A unicorn is a privately held startup valued at 1 billion US dollars or more. Investor Aileen Lee coined the term in 2013 when such companies were rare. Valuations are set in funding rounds and can fall sharply, so a unicorn is not the same as a profitable company.

title: Angel investors
body: Angels are wealthy individuals, often former founders, who invest their own money in very early startups, typically before VCs will. Besides cash they bring advice and introductions. Angel networks let several angels pool smaller cheques into one deal.

title: Bootstrapping
body: Bootstrapping means growing from your own savings and customer revenue instead of outside investors. You keep full ownership and control and must be profitable early, but growth is usually slower. Many great companies were bootstrapped for years before raising money.

title: The minimum viable product
body: An MVP is the simplest version of a product that lets you learn whether customers really want it. Instead of building for a year in secret, launch something small, measure what people actually do, and improve. It is a core idea of the lean startup method.

title: Build, measure, learn
body: The lean startup method treats a business as a set of guesses to test. Build a small experiment, measure real customer behaviour, learn, then persevere or pivot. The goal is to learn what works with as little time and money as possible.

title: CAC and LTV
body: Customer acquisition cost (CAC) is what you spend to win one customer. Lifetime value (LTV) is the gross profit that customer brings over time. A common rule of thumb is LTV at least 3 × CAC. If winning a customer costs more than they are worth, growth destroys money.

title: Burn rate and runway
body: Burn rate is how much cash a company loses each month. Runway = cash ÷ monthly burn. With 600,000 in the bank and a 50,000 monthly burn, you have 12 months to reach profit or raise again. Fundraising takes months, so start well before the money runs out.

title: Gross margin
body: Gross margin = (revenue − cost of goods sold) ÷ revenue. Software often has margins above 70%, because another copy costs almost nothing; retailers and manufacturers are often far lower. High margins leave more money for growth, which is one reason investors love software.

title: Revenue, profit and cash
body: Revenue is money earned from sales. Profit is what remains after costs. Cash is what is actually in the bank. A profitable company can still go bust if customers pay late while suppliers want paying now. That is why cash flow is watched weekly.

title: The break-even point
body: Break-even units = fixed costs ÷ (price − variable cost per unit). If rent and salaries cost 5,000 a month and each item sells for 10 with 6 of variable cost, you must sell 1,250 a month before making any profit.

title: Term sheets
body: A term sheet is the short summary of an investment deal: amount, valuation, share type, board seats, investor protections and conditions. Most of it is non-binding, but it sets the deal. Founders should read the control terms, not just the valuation.

title: Liquidation preference
body: A 1× liquidation preference means investors get their money back first when the company is sold, before common shareholders. If investors put in 10 million and the company sells for 12 million, founders and staff share only the remaining 2 million.

title: Vesting and the cliff
body: Founder and employee shares usually vest over four years with a one-year cliff: leave before 12 months and you get nothing; after that, shares vest monthly. It protects the company if a co-founder quits early while holding a large stake.

title: How investors get paid: exits
body: Startup shares are hard to sell, so investors get their return at an exit: an acquisition by a bigger company, or an initial public offering (IPO) that lists shares on a stock exchange. Most exits are acquisitions; IPOs are rarer and suit larger companies.

title: Network effects
body: A product has network effects when it gets more valuable as more people use it. WhatsApp, mobile money and marketplaces work this way. They are hard to start, since the first users get little value, but become very hard for rivals to beat.

title: Moats
body: A moat is a lasting advantage that protects profits from competitors: network effects, strong brands, high switching costs, patents, economies of scale or unique data. Investors ask 'what stops a bigger company copying you?' The moat is the answer.

title: SWOT analysis
body: SWOT lists a business's internal Strengths and Weaknesses and its external Opportunities and Threats. It is a quick way to structure strategy discussions: build on strengths, fix or avoid weaknesses, chase opportunities and prepare for threats.

title: The business model canvas
body: The business model canvas describes a business on one page in nine blocks: customer segments, value propositions, channels, customer relationships, revenue streams, key resources, key activities, key partners and cost structure.

title: Pricing strategies
body: Cost-plus pricing adds a margin to cost. Value-based pricing charges according to the value customers get, often far more profitable. Freemium gives a basic version free and charges for more. Subscriptions turn one-off sales into predictable recurring revenue.

title: Masiyiwa's fight for a licence
body: Strive Masiyiwa spent about five years fighting in Zimbabwe's courts for the right to launch a private mobile network. His win in the late 1990s led to Econet Wireless, which later launched EcoCash and grew into a pan-African telecoms and technology group.

title: African fintech unicorns
body: Africa's first startups valued at over 1 billion dollars were mostly in payments. Nigeria's Flutterwave, which helps businesses accept payments across Africa, reached a valuation of about 3 billion dollars in 2022. Payments is where Africa's biggest tech gaps meet huge demand.

title: Y Combinator
body: Y Combinator, founded in 2005, invests a small amount in many startups at once and coaches them for three months before a Demo Day with investors. Its alumni include Airbnb, Stripe, Dropbox and Coinbase, and it has funded several African startups.

title: Runway maths
body: Startup finance check.
statement: With 600,000 in cash and a 50,000 monthly burn, runway is 12 months

title: Post-money ownership
body: Valuation check.
statement: Investing 1 million at a 4 million pre-money valuation buys 25%
explanation: Post-money = 4 + 1 = 5 million, so the investor owns 1 ÷ 5 = 20%.

title: Revenue and profit
body: Business check.
statement: A business with fast-growing revenue is always profitable
explanation: Revenue can grow while costs grow faster. Many fast-growing startups lose money for years.

title: What a unicorn is
body: VC check.
statement: A unicorn is a private startup valued at 1 billion dollars or more
explanation: The term, coined in 2013, describes privately held startups valued at 1 billion US dollars or more.
